title: The loss of a child
hookLine: the Church entrusts children who die, born or unborn, to God's mercy
tomorrow: Mia's parents are splitting up. where does that leave her mom?

lines: IT WAITS FOR SOMEONE TO ASK.
cards: Some grief goes quiet for years, then speaks up at a kitchen table, during a long recovery, when there's finally time. A grandmother says a baby's name out loud that nobody at the table has heard before. Why now?
Because a loss like that doesn't expire. It waits for someone to ask. And under it sits a question as old as grief: where is my child now?

teach.b: Catholics answer with trust, not a map.

The Church entrusts children who die, born or unborn, to the mercy of God, and the Catechism points to Jesus's own words, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God."
One to tell a friend: limbo was a theory some theologians held for children who died unbaptized.
The Church never made it a teaching, and today it speaks of hope.
Scripture doesn't hide the grief, either: Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted. A neighbor tradition carries this loss too.
In a Buddhist story from the old commentaries, a young mother, Kisa Gotami, carries her dead son from house to house, begging for medicine.

teach.h: A MUSTARD SEED FROM EVERY DOOR.
teach.b: The Buddha tells her to bring one mustard seed from a home where no one has ever died. She knocks on door after door and finds no such home, and she understands she isn't alone.
What's shared: a grieving parent shouldn't stand alone, and every household knows loss.
An honest difference: the Buddha's answer turns her toward impermanence, that all things change. The Catholic answer entrusts the child to God, with the hope of being together again.

how: Catholic parishes offer funeral rites for children, including those who died before birth, and some families name the child and have a Mass offered; the Church entrusts children who die without baptism to God's mercy.

games.q: what does “the loss of a child” mean?
o: a child who stops practicing the faith
a child's death, and the grief that doesn't expire
a family drifting apart after an argument

games.q: grief, hope, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: a theory, never a Church teaching
a mustard seed from a home without loss

s: it was a theory some theologians held. the Church entrusts these children to God's mercy, with hope.
in the Buddhist story, Kisa Gotami finds no home where no one has died
she learns she isn't alone. the story turns her toward impermanence.
the Catholic and Buddhist answers to a child's death are the same
both say the grieving aren't alone. the Catholic answer entrusts the child to God; the story points to impermanence.

games.q: a coworker lost a pregnancy early on. she says she isn't sure she's 'allowed' to grieve, since the baby was never born. what fits today?
o: yes. her grief is real, and the Church entrusts children born or unborn to God.
it's better to move on quickly, since it happened so early.
only a baptized baby can be mourned by the Church.
games.why: the Church entrusts children who die, born or unborn, to God's mercy. a loss like that doesn't expire, and it can be mourned.

practice: If there's a candle or any small light near you, rest your eyes on it; if not, look toward a window. Bring to mind any parent who has lost a child, someone you know or someone you'll never meet.
Let the light stand for them while you breathe. If you pray, you can pray for them and for their child, by name if you know it.

wordCard.voice: The loss of a child. A grief that doesn't expire, and a child this tradition entrusts to the mercy of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the little children, in 'suffer the little children to come unto me.'

carryVoice: Keep this one gently: held by God, every one of them, named or unnamed. Rest well.

sources.q: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God.
